MUJAHID:v2p434#2/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p434#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p434#2/r1.claim: Mujahid defines the barzakh as the barrier between death and return to worldly life.

MUJAHID:v2p434#2/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p434#2/r2.speaker: الحسن
MUJAHID:v2p434#2/r2.claim: Al-Hasan says the barzakh is the graves that lie between people and the afterlife.

MUQATIL:23:100/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:23:100/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:23:100/r1.claim: The word the dying person says is his plea, Lord, send me back.

MUQATIL:23:100/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:23:100/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:23:100/r2.claim: A barzakh is the period after death that lasts until people are raised.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r1.speaker: الحسن
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r1.claim: Al-Hasan says anyone without God's friendship asks to return at death once the Fire becomes clear, even someone mute who never spoke; those nearby do not hear the request.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r2.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r2.claim: The request to return and do good in what was left behind is rejected; it parallels the dying person's request for more time to give charity.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r3.speaker: رسول الله
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r3.claim: A report from an unnamed man of Banū Ḥāritha says a dying person sees what had kept him from his obligations placed before him, prompting the plea to return; versions place these things before him or between his eyes.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r4.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r4.speaker: السدي
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p415/r4.claim: Al-Suddī says a dying unbeliever sees few good deeds and many bad ones, sees the Angel of Death, and wishes to return, then God says he will not return; descendants do not hear the utterance.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r1.speaker: مجاهد
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r1.claim: Mujāhid defines the barrier as the span between death and resurrection.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r2.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r2.claim: Qatāda says the people in graves are in the barrier between this world and the next.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r3.speaker: السدي
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p416/r3.claim: Al-Suddī says the barrier lasts from one trumpet blast to the next.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p48#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p48#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p48#2/r1.claim: Qatada defines the barzakh as the remainder of worldly life before resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v17p107/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r1.claim: At death the polytheist regrets neglected obedience and asks to return to worldly life so he can do the righteous deeds he abandoned.

TAB-FULL:v17p107/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r2.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r2.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī asks rhetorically what the dying person wants to return for—wealth, planting, building, or digging canals—before God answers “No.”

TAB-FULL:v17p107/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says the plea occurs as worldly life ends and the person sees the afterlife, before tasting death.

TAB-FULL:v17p107/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB-FULL:v17p107/r4.claim: A report to ʿĀʾisha says the believer who sees the angels rejects return to the house of grief, while the disbeliever asks to return and do good.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r1.claim: “It is a word he is saying” refers to the polytheist's plea “My Lord, return me”; the barzakh is a barrier before them preventing return until resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd says the dying person inevitably utters the plea and glosses the barzakh as a barrier ahead of them that prevents return.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r3.claim: Barzakh, barrier, and interval are near-synonyms here, lasting until people are raised from their graves on Judgment Day.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the barzakh as a term or appointed time until resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r5.speaker: سعيد
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r5.claim: Saʿīd says the barzakh is what comes after death.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r6.speaker: أبو أمامة
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r6.claim: At a burial, Abū Umāma called the grave a barzakh lasting until resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r7.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r7.claim: Mujahid defines the barzakh as the period from death until resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r8.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r8.claim: Mujahid also describes it as a barrier between the dead and their return to worldly life.

TAB-FULL:v17p109/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r9.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v17p109/r9.claim: Qatada says the barzakh is the remainder of worldly life before resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v17p111/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p111/r1.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v17p111/r1.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk defines the barzakh as the span between this world and the next.

ZAJJAJ:v4p21#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p21#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p21#2/r2.claim: كلا is a rebuke and alert; barzakh is the barrier between death and resurrection.

ZAJJAJ:v4p21#2/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p21#2/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p21#2/r3.claim: يوم is annexed to a verb because time nouns can be annexed to verbs.

NAHHAS:v3p121/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p121/r4.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p121/r4.claim: Barzakh is any barrier between two things; here it divides this world from the next.

NAHHAS:v3p121/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p121/r5.speaker: الشعبي
NAHHAS:v3p121/r5.claim: When a man said someone had become one of the people of the next life, al-Shaʿbī corrected him: he is in the intermediate barrier, neither this world nor the next.

NAHHAS:v3p121/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p121/r6.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p121/r6.claim: Yawm is a time adverb annexed to the verb of being raised; Abu Ishaq says the construction is essentially a quotation.

SULAMI:v2p39/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p39/r1.speaker: أبو عثمان
SULAMI:v2p39/r1.claim: If the damned knew what deeds could save them, they would plead to return and act righteously; obey God now, avoid spiritual claims, and correct one's practice, since abandoning the path leaves one stalled.

THALABI:v7p55/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p55/r10.speaker: الضحاك وابن زيد
THALABI:v7p55/r10.claim: They say barzakh is the period between death and resurrection.

THALABI:v7p55/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p55/r11.speaker: أبو أمامة
THALABI:v7p55/r11.claim: He identifies barzakh as the grave.

THALABI:v7p55/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p55/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p55/r6.claim: Barzakh is a barrier between death and return to worldly life until resurrection; ورائهم means before them.

THALABI:v7p55/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p55/r7.speaker: مجاهد وابن عباس
THALABI:v7p55/r7.claim: They explain barzakh as a barrier or veil.

THALABI:v7p55/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p55/r8.speaker: السدي
THALABI:v7p55/r8.claim: He interprets barzakh as a term or appointed time.

THALABI:v7p55/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p55/r9.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v7p55/r9.claim: He interprets barzakh as the remainder of worldly life.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r1.claim: Barzakh is a barrier ahead of the dead; the term is also used for the barrier between bodies of water.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r2.claim: Barzakh is the barrier between death and resurrection.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r3.speaker: الضحاك
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r3.claim: It is the barrier between this world and the next.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r4.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r4.claim: It prevents the dead from returning to this world.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r5.speaker: ابن عيسى
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r5.claim: It may mean the respite lasting until Resurrection.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r6.speaker: الكلبي
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p66/r6.claim: It is the term between trumpet blasts, with forty years between them.

QUSHAYRI:v2p350/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p350/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p350/r10.claim: On that Day, kinship and regret do not help; each person meets the result of what they earned, and acknowledgment and excuses come too late.

QUSHAYRI:v2p350/r11.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p350/r11.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p350/r11.claim: The damned acknowledge truth only on a day when admission and excuses do not benefit them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r1.claim: The righteous deed the dying person hopes to perform is bearing witness that there is no god but God.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r2.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r2.claim: Muqatil says the hoped-for righteous action means faith.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r3.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r3.claim: Qatada says the disbeliever did not wish to return to family or tribe, only to obey God; the living should take heed of that wish.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r4.claim: “In what I left behind” means the time already passed in his life.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r5.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r5.claim: Al-Kalbi explains it as the things the person denied.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r6.speaker: غيره
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r6.claim: Another interpreter says it means what he neglected.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r7.claim: “Never!” means he will not return to worldly life; the request is inevitably spoken at death when he sees God's punishment, as Ibn Zayd also says.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r8.speaker: آخرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p63/r8.claim: Others say the request is only empty speech: it brings no benefit because the speaker will not receive what he asks, like the two verses about saying things with one's mouth.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r1.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r1.claim: Abu Ubayda says “behind them” means ahead of them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r10.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r10.claim: Mujahid says it is a veil preventing their return to worldly life until resurrection.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r11.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r11.claim: Qatada says it is the remainder of worldly life: they stay in barzakh until the world ends and they are resurrected.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r12.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r12.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r12.claim: The pronoun in “behind them is a barzakh” refers to the same people as the preceding phrase “when one of them is reached by death.”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r2.claim: The phrase can mean between them as Abu Ubayda says, or behind them as in the earlier reference to Hell behind a person.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r3.claim: Barzakh literally means any barrier between two things, concrete or abstract, such as distance, a wall, days, or hostility.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r4.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r4.claim: Al-Farra says barzakh, barrier, and interval are close in meaning; the obstacle may be distance or something that prevents an event.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r5.speaker: علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r5.claim: A report says Ali omitted a barzakh during prayer, meaning the interval between the position he left and the position where he ended up.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r6.claim: The word also describes the boundary between certainty and doubt; a dead person is in barzakh because he lies between worldly life and the next life.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r7.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r7.claim: Abu Ishaq defines the barzakh here as the barrier between a person's death and resurrection; al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd say similarly.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas explains barzakh as a veil.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r9.speaker: السدي ومقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p64/r9.claim: Al-Suddi and Muqatil gloss barzakh as a fixed term or appointed span.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p66/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p66/r1.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p66/r1.claim: The time noun “day” is annexed to the verb “they are resurrected,” since Arabic permits temporal nouns to be annexed to verbs.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:96-101/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:96-101/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:96-101/r5.claim: The hoped-for good deed is bearing witness to divine unity; God refuses the request, and a barrier blocks return to the world until resurrection.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:96-101/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:96-101/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:96-101/r6.claim: Barzakh means a barrier between the dead and return to worldly life.

JISHUMI:v7p5089/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5089/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5089/r3.claim: Kallā is a rebuke and rejection; another analysis makes it negate what precedes and affirm what follows.

JISHUMI:v7p5089/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5089/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5089/r4.claim: Barzakh is a barrier or any division between two things.

JISHUMI:v7p5089/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5089/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5089/r5.claim: يوم is not nunated because it is annexed to a verb; time nouns can take verbal clauses as genitives, meaning the day of their resurrection.

JISHUMI:v7p5093/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5093/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5093/r3.claim: A report from the Prophet says that a believer asked by angels whether he wants to return to worldly sorrow declines and goes forward to God; the unbeliever asks for return as in these verses. No grading is stated.

JISHUMI:v7p5093/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5093/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5093/r4.claim: The dead ask to return and promise good works, showing their deeds and ability are their own; otherwise the request would be meaningless, refuting compulsion.

JISHUMI:v7p5093/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5093/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5093/r5.claim: There is no return to worldly life after death, contrary to the Imamis, and resurrection will occur.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r10.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r10.claim: He says he wants to make up the neglected testimony that there is no god but God; another view is that he wants to obey God.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r11.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r11.claim: He wants neither family nor worldly wealth and pleasures; he wishes to return only to obey God.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r12.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r12.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r12.claim: كلا rebukes the request: he will not return; it is merely a word he says and will not obtain.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r13.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r13.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r13.claim: Barzakh is a barrier preventing return to worldly life.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r14.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r14.claim: Barzakh means the remainder of worldly life.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r15.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r15.speaker: الضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r15.claim: Barzakh is the span from death to resurrection.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r16.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r16.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p428/r16.claim: Another interpretation identifies barzakh as the grave, where they remain until resurrection.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r10.claim: Barzakh is the barrier ahead of the dead until resurrection; it does not mean they return at resurrection, which is only a return to the afterlife.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r4.claim: “So that I may do good in what I left” means hoping to perform the faith omitted earlier, like building on a foundation means first laying that foundation.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r5.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r5.claim: Another explanation is that the dying person asks to return to use the wealth he left behind.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r6.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r6.claim: A report says that a believer offered return by the angels refuses the world of troubles and asks to proceed to God, while the unbeliever says, “Lord, return me.”

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r7.claim: Kalla rebukes and rejects the request to return.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r8.claim: “The word” means this connected portion of speech, the request to do good in what was left.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p205/r9.claim: “He will say it” means he cannot stop repeating it under grief and regret, or that only he says it and no answer is granted.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r4.claim: A report to Aisha says the believer, when seeing death, chooses to go forward to God rather than return to the house of grief, while the unbeliever asks to return and do good.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r5.speaker: الحسن والجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r5.claim: Al-Hasan and the majority use a still yā in laʿalli; Talha b. Musarrif opens it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r6.claim: Kalla is a divine rejection and rebuke; the phrase that follows has three possible senses: a prediction, an empty utterance, or proof that a returned person would relapse.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r7.claim: Barzakh literally means a barrier between two distances and here denotes the period between death and resurrection, as the exegetes agree.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p155#2/r8.claim: The majority read al-sur as the trumpet; Ibn Abbas reads al-suwar with a fatḥa on the wāw, meaning images or forms.

TABRISI:23:100/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:100/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:23:100/r1.claim: The first explanation makes those in the barzakh separated from the world until the day of resurrection; the dead remain there until they are raised.

TABRISI:23:100/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:100/r2.speaker: علي بن عيسى
TABRISI:23:100/r2.claim: Ali ibn Isa says barzakh is a period of respite until Judgment Day, identified with the grave; more generally, any division between two things is a barzakh.

TABRISI:23:100/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:100/r3.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:23:100/r3.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi infers that at death each person necessarily learns his station with God and whether he belongs among the rewarded or punished.

TABRISI:23:100/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:100/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
TABRISI:23:100/r4.claim: Barzakh is a barrier between death and resurrection, preventing the dead from returning until the day they are raised.

TABRISI:23:96-100/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:96-100/r10.speaker: العياشي
TABRISI:23:96-100/r10.claim: Al-ʿAyyashi transmits that al-Fatḥ ibn Yazid asked al-Riḍā whether God knows counterfactual events; the Imam says the difficult question is answered by God's knowing what disbelievers claim would happen if they returned, though they would repeat their wrongdoing.

TABRISI:23:96-100/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:96-100/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:23:96-100/r11.claim: ‘No’ rejects return to worldly life; the plea is only a spoken phrase without benefit, as shown by the statement that returned disbelievers would repeat what they had been forbidden.

TABRISI:23:96-100/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:96-100/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:23:96-100/r8.claim: The dying person asks to do good with what he left behind, meaning to pay God's due from his estate, to use his worldly life for good, or to make up neglected prayers, fasting, and acts of worship.

TABRISI:23:96-100/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:23:96-100/r9.speaker: الصادق
TABRISI:23:96-100/r9.claim: Al-Sadiq says this plea is made by someone who withheld the obligatory alms and seeks to return to pay it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r1.claim: What the dying person left behind means the remaining span of his life.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r2.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r2.claim: Alternatively, he means the good deeds he left undone.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r3.claim: Kallā rejects the request: he will not return to the world; it is merely an empty word with no benefit to him.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r4.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r4.claim: Barzakh is the interval between this world and the next; anything between two things is a barzakh.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r5.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p490/r5.claim: Barzakh literally means a barrier, here the interval between a person's death and resurrection.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r10.speaker: رسول الله
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r10.claim: The Prophet's report says a believer seeing the angels declines return to worldly grief, while a disbeliever wants it for money, farming, buildings, or waterways; God refuses.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r11.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r11.claim: A second reading treats “No!” as confirming that the reported plea really is the word he will utter.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r12.claim: Al-Razi prefers “No!” as a refusal of the requested return.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r5.claim: “Perhaps” does not express doubt: the speaker is resolved to obey if returned, like someone certain he will repair a known failure.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r6.claim: Alternatively, because the future is unknown, people use wording of hope rather than certainty; the Qur'an says returned people would repeat their old conduct.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r7.claim: Some read “what I left” as the wealth left behind, from which the returned person could pay God's due.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r8.claim: Others take it more broadly as all neglected duties, bodily and financial worship and rights; this better fits their wish to repair every wrong and disobedience.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104#2/r9.claim: One reading of “No!” is a refusal of their request, like telling an implausible petitioner “never.” A report to Aisha contrasts the believer's refusal with the disbeliever's request.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says one who neglected charity and pilgrimage asks to return at death; when challenged that only disbelievers ask, he cites the warning to spend before death.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r2.speaker: رسول الله
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r2.claim: The Prophet says that, as death approaches, a person sees all the rights he had withheld brought before him and asks to return and act righteously.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r3.claim: The request is by disbelievers: believers who see their place in Paradise would not wish for more, while the least rewarded would otherwise grieve over higher ranks.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r4.claim: The cited warning to spend before death describes worldly life, not the state of reward, so it does not overturn the preferred reading.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r5.claim: Most interpreters place the request at the moment of death's direct apprehension, when the person is compelled to recognize God and his disobedience.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r6.claim: Others place the request when the condemned see Hell in the afterlife, drawing on other descriptions of Hell's inhabitants asking to return.

RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p104/r7.claim: The verse itself attaches the request to death's arrival, so there is no reason to abandon that apparent timing, even if they later ask again.

RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r1.claim: One reading says the speaker keeps repeating the plea, unable to fall silent under the force of remorse.

RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r2.claim: Another says he alone utters the plea, but it receives no answer and is not heard.

RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r3.claim: Barzakh means a barrier or restraint, as between two seas; death blocks reconciliation and reunion until resurrection, without implying return to worldly life then.

RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p105/r4.claim: The mention of resurrection completely extinguishes hope of return, since the only return then is to the afterlife.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r1.claim: The words may instead refer to God: His promise cannot fail, and He has said no soul is delayed past its term and that this disbeliever will not believe; alternatively the dying person utters them, but they do not help.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r2.speaker: الضحاك ومجاهد وابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r2.claim: They define barzakh as a barrier between death and Resurrection; Mujahid also calls it the barrier between death and return to earthly life.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r3.speaker: الضحاك وابن عباس والسدي وقتادة وابن عيسى والكلبي
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r3.claim: Further definitions are the interval between worlds, a veil, a term, what remains of worldly life, respite until Resurrection, or the period between the two trumpet blasts, said to be forty years; the author calls these close.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r4.speaker: الجوهري
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r4.claim: Al-Jawhari defines barzakh as a barrier; the author says every barrier between two things is a barzakh and every dead person enters the interval from death to Resurrection.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r5.speaker: الشعبي
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r5.claim: Al-Shaʿbi corrects a man who says the deceased has joined the next life: he has entered barzakh, neither this world nor the next.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100#2/r6.claim: The time word is annexed to they are raised because it is a time adverb, with the annexation expressing the verbal noun.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas explains what was left behind as the testimony that there is no god but God.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r8.claim: The phrase may mean acts of worship he neglected, or the wealth he left that he could have given in charity; laʿalla signals uncertainty about being returned or enabled to act if returned.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:23:99-100/r9.claim: Kallā rejects the presumed return: his plea will be thrown away; even if returned, he would not fulfill the promise, as the verse about their return says.

BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r1.claim: He hopes to do good in what he left behind, meaning faith he failed to embrace, or perhaps his property or worldly life.

BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r2.claim: The Prophet reports that a believer seeing the angels declines a return to life's sorrows and griefs, while an unbeliever asks to return.

BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r3.claim: The word kalla rebukes and rules out return; the dying person's plea is a speech he will inevitably utter in regret.

BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:100/r4.claim: A barzakh separates them from returning until resurrection, ruling out any return to earthly life even at the Resurrection.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r1.claim: He asks to return to the world he left; Qatāda says he seeks neither family nor clan, only a chance to repair his neglect.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r2.claim: The Kāfī, Sahl, and Yaʿqūb readings leave the yāʾ in “laʿallī” still.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r3.claim: “Never” rejects and dismisses the request; “word” denotes the whole connected utterance that he will inevitably say in remorse.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p130#6/r4.claim: “Behind them” means before them; the barrier between them and return lasts until resurrection and rules out any return after it as well.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p577#3/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p577#3/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p577#3/r2.claim: Barzakh is an intervening barrier between two distances or things that keeps one from reaching the other.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r6.claim: “In what I left” can mean the faith abandoned: the dying person hopes to perform the good he omitted, like someone who says he will build on a foundation, meaning first lay one.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also interprets what was left behind as wealth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r8.claim: “No” rejects and rules out the request to return; it may be God's rebuke or the dying person's self-reproach, whose repeated words are useless and unanswered.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p583/r9.claim: The barzakh is a barrier preventing disbelievers' return until resurrection; it makes return to worldly life wholly hopeless and names the period between death and resurrection metaphorically.

SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r1.claim: كلمة uses a part for the whole utterance, as in the report that the truest word of a poet is Labid's line that all things perish except God.

SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r2.claim: هو قائلها is an adjective describing كلمة.

SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r3.claim: برزخ is a barrier between incompatible things, or more generally a partition preventing two things from meeting; these senses are equivalent.

SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r4.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:23:100/r4.claim: Al-Raghib traces برزخ to Persian برزه, says it separates a person from high stations in the afterlife, and before resurrection bars the dead from returning.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r1.claim: Kallā is a rebuke and deterrent: God will neither grant the dying person's request to return nor accept it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r2.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r2.claim: Every dying wrongdoer inevitably utters this request.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r3.claim: Alternatively, the request is merely speech without action; even if returned, the person would not act righteously and would be lying, as 6:28 says.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r4.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r4.claim: He portrays the dying person asking to return, then God answers that this is only a word he says.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r5.speaker: عمر بن عبد الله مولى غفرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r5.claim: When God says kallā, it means that the speaker has lied.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r6.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r6.claim: Qatāda transmits al-Alāʾ ibn Ziyād's advice to imagine death has arrived and one's request for reprieve was granted, then obey God.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r7.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r7.claim: The unbeliever longs to return for obedience to God, not to rejoin family or tribe; the living should act on that wish.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r8.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r8.claim: A dead unbeliever sees his place in the Fire, asks to return and repent, but is told his allotted life is over; the grave then constricts and its creatures torment him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r9.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493#2/r9.claim: A report from ʿĀʾisha describes black or dark snakes biting sinful people in their graves until they meet at the body's middle, identifying this as barzakh punishment.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493/r1.claim: At death, unbelievers and those who neglected God's commands ask to return to worldly life so they can repair what they ruined; they are refused. The same plea appears in 63:10–11, 14:44, 7:53, 32:12, 6:27–28, 42:44, 40:11–12, and 35:37.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p493/r2.claim: They are denied a return at the moment of death, at resurrection, during judgment before the Lord, and when shown the Fire; they remain amid the throes of Hell's punishment.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r1.speaker: أبو صالح وغيره
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r1.claim: They explain min warāʾihim as meaning ahead of them.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r2.claim: Mujāhid defines the barzakh as the barrier between this world and the next.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r3.speaker: محمد بن كعب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r3.claim: The dead are between the two worlds: neither sharing worldly eating and drinking nor receiving the next life's recompense.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r4.speaker: أبو صخر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r4.claim: Abū Ṣakhr identifies the barzakh with the graves, where people remain between worldly life and the afterlife until resurrection.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r5.claim: The barzakh is a threat of its punishment to these dying wrongdoers, like the threats of Hell and a severe punishment behind people in 45:10 and 14:17.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p494/r6.claim: Barzakh punishment continues until resurrection; a hadith says the dead person continues to be punished in the earth.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r4.claim: The dying person hopes to return only to believe and do the good he left undone, rather than to rejoin family or gather wealth and satisfy desires.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r5.speaker: قتادة
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r5.claim: Al-Baghawi reports Qatada's view that the dying person's sole wish is to return to obey God, not to family, kin, wealth, or pleasure.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r6.speaker: العلاء بن زياد
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r6.claim: Ibn Kathir reports al-ʿAlaʾ ibn Ziyad urging anyone who imagines death has arrived and asks God for respite to act now in obedience.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r7.claim: Kallā decisively denies any return: the request is merely a word the person utters, known from his past deceit and lacking genuine resolve.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p221/r8.claim: The barzakh is an unremovable barrier surrounding the dead between worldly life and resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v6p114/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p114/r4.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v6p114/r4.claim: Aisha describes black snakes in sinners’ graves striking the head and feet until they meet in the middle; she identifies this as punishment in the barzakh.

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r10.speaker: أبو صخر
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r10.claim: Abu Sakhr calls the barzakh the cemeteries, where the dead remain until resurrection, belonging neither to this world nor the next.

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r11.speaker: أبو أمامة
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r11.claim: At a burial, Abu Umama said the grave is a barzakh until resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r4.speaker: سفيان بن حسين
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r4.claim: Sufyan ibn Husayn glosses ‘behind them’ as ‘before them.’

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r5.claim: Mujahid describes the barzakh as the interval and barrier from death to resurrection, preventing the dead from returning to worldly life.

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r6.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r6.claim: The barzakh is between this world and the next: its people neither share worldly eating and drinking nor yet receive recompense for their deeds.

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r7.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r7.claim: Al-Hasan says the barzakh lies between this world and the next.

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r8.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r8.claim: Qatada calls the barzakh the remainder of worldly life; he also says grave-dwellers remain in it until resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v6p115/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r9.speaker: الربيع
DURR-FULL:v6p115/r9.claim: Al-Rabiʿ identifies the barzakh as the graves.

DURR-FULL:v6p116/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p116/r1.speaker: الشعبي
DURR-FULL:v6p116/r1.claim: Al-Shaʿbi says the deceased is neither in this world nor the next, but in the barzakh.

DURR-FULL:v6p116/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p116/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v6p116/r2.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr glosses the barzakh as what comes after death.

BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r4.claim: He imagines being asked whether he wants to return to gather wealth, plant, build, or dig canals, then says he wants to do righteous work with the faith he left behind.

BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r5.claim: He does not frame faith itself as a hope because he presents it as definite, while righteous action is what he hopes to perform.

BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r6.speaker: الجلالين
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r6.claim: Al-Jalalayn interprets the hoped-for righteous work as testifying to God's oneness, which he left undone in worldly life.

BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r7.speaker: بعضهم
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r7.claim: One view addresses the Angel of Death and his helpers; the mention of Lord is an oath, and the man appeals first to God and then to the angels.

BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r8.speaker: النبي عليه السلام
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r8.claim: A report says a believer who sees the angels declines return to the world and welcomes going to God, whereas an unbeliever asks to be returned.

BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r9.speaker: الكبير
BURSEVI:v6p74#3/r9.claim: Al-Kabir considers فيما تركت broader: it includes neglected worship and both bodily and financial duties or rights.

BURSEVI:v6p75#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p75#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p75#3/r1.claim: The barzakh lasts until resurrection and wholly rules out returning to worldly life; the return at resurrection is to the afterlife.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r1.claim: ‘In what I left behind’ may mean abandoned faith; laʿalla may express hope about both work and faith despite knowing return will not happen, or only work because faith on return is certain.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r10.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that the dying person says kallā to himself; kallā and what follows are God’s speech.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r11.claim: Warāʾahum means ‘before them’; the pronoun refers to one dying person in wording but to all in meaning.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r12.claim: Barzakh is a barrier between the dead and return, lasting until they are raised.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r2.claim: Alternatively, what was left is wealth or worldly life; laʿalla may also express purpose.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r3.speaker: البغوي عن الواقدي
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r3.claim: Al-Baghawī cites al-Wāqidī that every Qur’anic laʿalla signals purpose except ‘perhaps you will live forever’ (26:129); al-Suddī’s route from Abū Mālik says similarly.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r4.claim: The wish to return is not confined to unbelievers: Ibn ʿAbbās says one who withheld zakāt or could afford pilgrimage but did not do it asks to return at death.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r5.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r5.claim: A Prophetic report through al-Daylamī from Jābir says at death things obstructing truth appear before a person’s eyes, prompting the plea to return; this supports reading what was left as wealth.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r6.claim: Kallā rebukes and dismisses the request to return as impossible.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r7.claim: ‘It is a word he says’ means the dying person inevitably utters it in regret; fronting the subject gives emphasis or exclusivity.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r8.claim: The lone-word phrase depicts futile speech receiving no answer, like the retort to occupy oneself alone with pointless speech; kalimah means speech.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p63#2/r9.claim: Grammarians treat kalimah meaning ‘speech’ as figurative, while lexicographers consider it literal or familiar metaphor.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r1.claim: The barzakh lasts from the graves until resurrection, making worldly return impossible like a camel passing through a needle’s eye.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd defines the barzakh as a barrier between death and resurrection, spanning the wait before people rise from graves.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p64/r3.claim: A further view makes the barzakh a barrier to complete requital that remains until Judgment Day, when full recompense comes.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r7.claim: The clause of hope gives the reason for the request to be returned.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r8.claim: Tark may retain its literal sense of leaving: what the speaker left behind is the world.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p122/r9.claim: Alternatively, figurative rejection means the faith in God and His messenger that the unbeliever refused; the plea promises obedience and admits past error.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r1.claim: Kallā rebukes the listener and signals that the unbeliever’s request is invalid.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r2.claim: The clause that it is merely a word is a Quranic, proverbial construction: the request is only speech and will not be answered.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r3.claim: Since it is obvious he says the word, the description means it has no quality beyond being uttered; inna emphasizes that point.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r4.claim: Kalima means utterance, as in the Prophetic report quoting Labīd and in the formulas for the testimony and Islam; 9:74 uses it similarly.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r5.claim: Warāʾ is a metaphor for something inevitably approaching and reaching someone unaware, like a pursuer catching up; examples occur in 85:20, 45:10, 14:17, and 18:79.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r6.speaker: لبيد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r6.claim: Labīd’s verse uses warāʾ for what lies ahead as one’s death approaches.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r7.claim: Barzakh means a barrier between two places; reported interpretations are the grave, the remaining span of worldly life, or an intermediate realm where souls see their future station, favored by Sufis.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r8.speaker: السيد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p123/r8.claim: Al-Sayyid’s Definitions calls barzakh the perceptible realm between abstract meanings and material bodies, or the imaginal world in ancient philosophy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p124/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p124/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p124/r1.claim: Until they are raised means the dead will not return to life before resurrection, extinguishing their hope because they know resurrection brings no return to worldly life.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r1.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r1.claim: Al-Qummi reports from al-Sadiq that barzakh is an intermediate state of reward and punishment between worldly life and the hereafter, and that the Imam fears for people concerning barzakh.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r2.speaker: علي بن الحسين
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r2.claim: Al-Sajjad says a grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of Fire.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r3.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r3.claim: Al-Sadiq rejects the claim that believers' spirits are inside green birds around the Throne: believers are too honored for this and dwell in bodies like their own.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r4.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r4.claim: One report says believers' spirits dwell in a tree in Paradise, eating and drinking while asking God to hasten the Hour and join later believers with earlier ones.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r5.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r5.claim: Another report places spirits in body-like forms in a Paradise tree, where they recognize one another and ask about those still living or dead.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:23:99-118#5/r6.claim: Reports detailing barzakh and the conditions of believers and others there are numerous and mutawatir, with some already discussed in earlier sections.

TABATABAI:23:99-118/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:23:99-118/r1.claim: “Behind them” means ahead and surrounding them: the future is said to be behind a person because it approaches and overtakes him.

TABATABAI:23:99-118/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:23:99-118/r2.claim: The barzakh is the grave realm, an imaginal life after death until Resurrection, supported by the context, other verses, and abundant Shiite and Sunni reports.

TABATABAI:23:99-118/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118/r3.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:23:99-118/r3.claim: Some say the barrier merely prevents return to worldly life until Resurrection; al-Tabataba'i rejects this because the context places the barrier between death and Resurrection and the time limit would be pointless.

ASAD-NOTES:23:99#n61/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:23:99#n61/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:23:99#n61/r1.claim: What the speaker left behind includes both neglected good deeds and wrongful deeds committed.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r2.claim: The opponents persist in mischief until death, then awaken to the next world; their plea to return is futile because the time for action ended at death and a barrier lasts until resurrection.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r3.claim: An alternative reading takes the words to mean that the speaker may utter this plea but would repeat his former conduct if returned.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p282/r4.claim: Although parallel Qur'anic passages support the alternative, the author prefers the reading that the plea is regret which cannot avail the dead.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r1.claim: ‘They’ especially means unbelievers who deny resurrection; only after death, when worldly ties and desires end, do they recognize their mistake and express despair and regret.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r2.speaker: Fahreddin er-Râzî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r2.claim: Razi says they cry out at death—or, in a weak view, on seeing their place in Hell—knowing return is impossible but grieving that they died unbelievers.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r3.claim: The verses explicitly reject reincarnation, an idea traced to ancient Indian religions and Plato: if souls could migrate between bodies until purified, God would not refuse the sinners’ request to return and correct their lives.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r4.speaker: Râzî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r4.claim: Razi prefers the common Islamic meaning of barzakh: death and what follows, which blocks return to worldly life until resurrection.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r5.speaker: Taberî ve Şevkânî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:99/r5.claim: Another explanation makes barzakh the interval between the two trumpet blasts, marking the end of worldly life and the resurrection.

QIRAAT-ER:23:100:1#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:23:100:1#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:23:100:1#1/r1.claim: Fatḥa on final yāʾ changes prosody but not core meaning; both forms are canonical.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p191/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p191/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p191/r1.claim: The dying person in al-Mu'minun asks to do righteous work, not specifically to give charity; this shows righteousness is the basis of salvation outside a passage about wealth.

STUDYQURAN:23:99/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r1.claim: The opening 'Till' continues the rejection recounted in 23:83: disbelievers persist in it until death comes.

STUDYQURAN:23:99/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r2.claim: Other verses likewise portray the dead seeking return so they may give charity or do righteous deeds.

STUDYQURAN:23:99/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r3.speaker: Some commentators
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r3.claim: Some commentators place the plea before death: after addressing God, the dying person asks the soul-taking angels to return him.

STUDYQURAN:23:99/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r4.speaker: Others (R)
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r4.claim: Other commentators place the request after death, when the person has seen the Fire.

STUDYQURAN:23:99/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r5.claim: The barzakh is an intervening barrier or isthmus, and the dead cannot return to worldly life.

STUDYQURAN:23:99/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r6.claim: Barzakh can mean either a barrier or an isthmus between two things.

STUDYQURAN:23:99/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r7.speaker: Some commentators (Ṭ)
STUDYQURAN:23:99/r7.claim: Some commentators explain that the dying person's words are words he could not help uttering.

STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r7.claim: The opposition of affluent and powerful people to prophets recurs throughout this surah, as elsewhere in the Quran.

STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r9.claim: The conclusion warns that disbelievers facing their perdition will wish to return to do good instead of evil, but it will be too late.
